sources.news_title: Trump says U.S. will not resume military strikes on Iran before Nov. 3 midterm elections
sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Thursday (October 8, 2026) that he will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the November 3 midterm elections in the United States.
Mr. Trump, while stumping for Republicans this week, has hinted that he was confident that an endgame to the war could come in the days before or after the election, while also hinting that he remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran.
For weeks, Mr. Trump has been threatening that a post-midterm election escalation in the seven-month-old war remains a viable option, despite his initial promises to Americans of a military campaign that would last a matter of weeks.
But Mr. Trump in a social media post on Thursday (October 8, 2026) said the U.S. “will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd”.
Mr. Trump added that his team has been “having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran.”
The U.S. and Iran signed a short-lived interim agreement in June, intended to establish a 60-day ceasefire and framework for a permanent peace deal.
The deal signed by Mr. Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian collapsed within weeks amid renewed military actions and disputes over control of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical water which one-fifth world's oil flowed through before the war.
Negotiations had appeared at a standstill since Mr. Trump late last month publicly rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the strait within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions.
Iran, however, said last week they had received a U.S. counterproposal. And Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi earlier on Thursday said he expected Tehran would offer a formal reply within days.
Mr. Trump on Wednesday (October 7, 2026) during a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, said that his special envoy, Steve Witkoff, has continued indirect negotiations with Iranian officials.
But at the same time, Mr. Trump suggested he had mixed feelings about ending the war at this point.
“I think the deal isn't really something that I want to do, but they're willing to offer us anything to stop,” Mr. Trump said.
Mr. Trump believes that America is gaining leverage as the U.S. military is having greater success in helping oil tankers traverse the Strait of Hormuz and get Gulf allies' oil to market, while a Navy blockade is shutting down Iran's own oil exports.
Iran has lost its near chokehold over oil flows through the vital waterway with U.S. Central Command shepherding oil tankers through the strait at night with their location systems turned off.
That with the help of Gulf pipelines that skirt the strait, has allowed Gulf countries to export oil at nearly prewar levels.
But Iran has ramped up attacks on tankers passing through the strait in recent days. And overall, ship traffic remains well below prewar levels, as are shipments of liquid natural gas and fuel products.
Tanker operators willing to risk running the gauntlet under Central Command's protection are in some cases charging rates of $1 million a day or more, shipping analysts say.
The situation has become further complicated as Saudi Arabia and Yemen's government have launched a military campaign aimed at driving Iran-backed Houthi rebels from the Bab el-Mandeb strait, another critical West Asia trade route for oil and other goods.
The Houthis, in turn, are targeting Saudi airports and key infrastructure in the kingdom with drone and missile strikes.
Mr. Trump's post comes as the military has dispatched more resources to the region. U.S. officials have said a third aircraft carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, and thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive as early as the end of October.
Mr. Trump's announcement was made the same day the USS Abraham Lincoln was due to arrive to its home port in San Diego after a record-long deployment in support of the Iran war. There have been reports of crew stress and poor mental health, as well as supply shortages, including food and hygiene products.
The USS George Washington, which is usually based in Asia, relieved the Lincoln in August. The other aircraft carrier in the West Asia, the USS George HW Bush, has been deployed for about six months, but it pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit several days ago.

sources.news_title: Trump rules out new Iran attack before US midterms
sources.text:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday ruled out attacking Iran before midterm elections on November 3, saying Washington was holding "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's post on his Truth Social platform followed a surge in oil prices on Thursday driven by media reports suggesting potential new US strikes prior to those elections.
"I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect...we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," he wrote.
"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," he added, without providing additional details.
The Atlantic magazine reported on Wednesday that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop options to strike Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms.
The New York Times published a similar report on Thursday, saying the plans were being developed despite Trump's "ambivalence".
The rise in crude oil prices has also been fuelled by persistent tensions in the Strait of Hormuz – a strategic chokepoint for the global oil trade – as well as hostilities between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia.
In a recent sign of those tensions, an oil tanker sailing off the north coast of Qatar reported being struck "by multiple projectiles," causing an unspecified number of casualties, the UKMTO maritime agency said Wednesday.
Polls suggest that US voters are strongly dissatisfied over rising fuel prices, linked to the conflict launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in February.
The US leader has repeatedly insisted in recent weeks that the United States has effectively won the Iran war, despite ongoing unrest and a recent security threat that forced the withdrawal of American bombers from a base in England.
But Trump's claims that prices will fall as soon as the Iran war is over have so far fallen on deaf ears with voters.
The midterm elections will shape the final two years of Trump's presidential term as his Republican Party risks losing its current grip on Congress. Although Trump is not on the ballot, he is heavily involved in the campaign, holding numerous rallies in an attempt to limit the damage or even turn the political tide.
Trump has warned he faces a possible third impeachment if Democrats retake the House of Representatives, and the White House is preparing for a slew of investigations into corruption and abuse of power.
The US president also on Thursday sought to calm a furore over his comments at a rally earlier this week that Iran could "take out" the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego.
Trump, 80, blamed the "fake and artificial news" for misinterpreting the remarks, which Democrats pounced on.
"In actuality, what I was talking about was that a temporary increase in the price of Gasoline is a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon and, if you want to see a big price, can you imagine what it would be like if they bombed San Diego and/or Los Angeles?" Trump said on Truth Social. (AFP)

Oil jumps 5%, then pares gains after Trump says no attack on Iran in October
Shell, Chevron, BP curtail Gulf of Mexico output over Hurricane Isaias threat
[HOUSTON] Oil prices jumped more than 5 per cent on Thursday (Oct 8), then pared gains after US President Donald Trump said the US will not launch an attack on Iran before midterm congressional elections in November.
Brent crude futures were up US$3.48, or 3.5 per cent, at US$103.73 a barrel by 12:41 pm ET (1641 GMT). US West Texas Intermediate crude gained US$2.69, or 3.1 per cent, to US$91.
At their session highs, both contracts were up more than US$5 a barrel, with Brent at its highest since Sep 29 on worries about potential imminent US strikes on Iran and a supply loss in the US Gulf of Mexico from Hurricane Isaias.
Then, Trump said Washington was having productive discussions with Iran.
The Tasnim news agency reported that Foreign Minister Abbas Araqhchi said Teheran is reviewing the US response to its proposal under which the Strait of Hormuz could be reopened within seven days, and could reply within days.
Syria was considering providing military assistance to key ally Saudi Arabia for its conflict with the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.
Options being considered include defensive aid or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops, the sources said.
Supply disruptions persist
On Wednesday, oil prices settled lower after the International Energy Agency agreed to accelerate the release of oil stocks and prioritise diesel supplies as governments seek to tackle record fuel prices and war-related supply disruptions.
“Further details surrounding the G7’s proposed 100 million-barrel SPR release have disappointed the market, as the barrels appear to be drawn from the previously announced 400 million-barrel release that has yet to be fully marketed,” Staunovo added.
Threats to oil shipping in the Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz, which carried shipments equal to about 20 per cent of global oil and fuel before the war, have increased in October as the Iran conflict enters its eighth month, boosting prices.
Attacks on tankers sailing through the strait last week hit their highest level since the war began, as Gulf producers increased exports.
“The frequency of Iranian attacks on ships is now at the highest point since the war began, and likely to intensify further,” said Saul Kavonic, MST Marquee head of energy.
“Constrained product flows, extreme logistics costs and high likelihood of Iranian escalation are keeping prices elevated.”
Hurricane Isaias
Also boosting prices, a hurricane moved toward US offshore production areas, causing companies to shut their platforms in the world’s biggest oil-producing country.
On Wednesday, Shell and Chevron said they were curtailing offshore operations in the Gulf as Hurricane Isaias approached. BP said it has removed all personnel from Na Kika and Thunder Horse platforms and shut in production at both.
Overall, US Gulf of Mexico oil and gas producers had shut in about 25.08 per cent of current oil production and 16.37 per cent of current natural gas production as of Wednesday because of the storm, according to the Marine Minerals Administration.
Inventory data from the US, also the world’s biggest oil consumer, supported prices as crude stockpiles fell by a higher-than-expected amount, while diesel inventories declined slightly. REUTERS

President Trump declared on Thursday that the United States would not launch military strikes against Iran prior to the midterm elections scheduled for November 3rd, according to a post on Truth Social. The president characterized discussions with Iran as productive and described the country’s economic and military conditions as deteriorating.
Trump claimed that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global waterway, had reached record volumes of 22 million barrels the previous night with no Iranian involvement. This assertion could not be independently verified. The strait has been a focal point of US policy, with Washington implementing a blockade beginning in April after failed negotiations in Islamabad, then reinstating restrictions in July following the collapse of a brief ceasefire agreement.
The military conflict between the US and Iran has seen several escalations, including strikes on Iranian positions in early September followed by Iranian missile responses targeting American bases in Jordan and the United Arab Emirates. Trump’s public messaging regarding the war has evolved over recent weeks. On September 2, he stated he was unaffected by electoral considerations, though he sought to support his party. By the following week, ahead of a Republican midterm convention in Dallas, he predicted the conflict would conclude shortly after voting concluded.
According to a Reuters/Ipsos survey from late September, approximately one-third of Americans approved of the strikes on Iran, while over 80 percent anticipated an extended conflict. Republican approval for Trump declined from 82 percent to 73 percent within a single week. Polling averages showed Democrats leading Republicans by approximately nine points on generic congressional ballot measures, marking the widest Democratic advantage recorded during the election cycle.
The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio had privately cautioned Trump that the conflict could extend throughout his presidency. Trump’s announcement did not address what US policy would entail following the November 3rd election date.

Bitcoin reclaims $81K as Trump rules out pre-midterm Iran strikes
Bitcoin has reclaimed $81,000 after U.S. President Donald Trump ruled out attacks on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, while oil prices have retreated following his statement.
- Bitcoin recovered above $81,000 following Trump’s statement, according to TradingView data cited in the report.
- Trump said discussions with Iran were productive, while maintaining the U.S. blockade.
- Polymarket traders assigned a 60% chance to the ceasefire lasting through Nov. 15.
- Iran’s foreign minister said Tehran would respond to Washington’s proposal within the next few days.
President Donald Trump said in an Oct. 8 Truth Social post that Washington was holding productive discussions with Tehran and would not attack Iran before Americans vote on Nov. 3. Alongside the pledge, he said the blockade would remain in force and repeated his position that Iran must not obtain a nuclear weapon.
Bitcoin recovers $81K after Trump’s statement
According to TradingView data cited in the supplied report, Bitcoin moved back above $81,000 after Trump’s announcement. PrimeXBT’s Oct. 8 market report also recorded the recovery and said oil prices pulled back following the president’s remarks.
In the same report, PrimeXBT described a volatile session in which Bitcoin had fallen below $81,000 for the first time since Sep. 21. More than $480 million in crypto positions were liquidated within one hour, with long positions accounting for most of the losses, according to the trading platform.
Earlier reporting shows that pressure from the conflict had already interrupted Bitcoin’s September recovery. On Sep. 28, crypto.news reported Bitcoin’s pullback below $84,000 after its previous week’s advance above $87,000, while renewed uncertainty over Iran weighed on markets.
According to that report, Trump had rejected an Iranian proposal involving a seven-day reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and a pause in fighting before talks on unresolved issues. During comments that Sunday, he said the conflict could end soon but declined to rule out military action before the midterms.
Trump keeps the blockade while ruling out attacks
In Thursday’s post, Trump described the diplomatic contacts as “productive discussions,” according to Ynetnews, which reproduced his statement. He also said Iran remained under economic and military pressure while the U.S. blockade continued.
Trump claimed that 22 million barrels of oil had passed through the Strait of Hormuz the previous night, with none entering or leaving Iran. His post presented the volume as a record and said the blockade would remain fully effective.
The president’s pledge followed reports that military officials were preparing options for renewed attacks. Ynetnews reported, citing Axios, that U.S. Central Command had been instructed several days earlier to complete preparations for a possible return to major combat operations, although Trump had made no final decision and no date had been set.
In separate coverage, Ynetnews said NBC News had reported discussions between Trump and his national security team about large-scale operations within weeks. The publication also cited The Atlantic’s reporting that the Pentagon had been asked to prepare possible strike options before the election.
According to The Atlantic’s account, as relayed by Ynetnews, officials were still considering the operation’s scope, and a more substantial military campaign could follow after the vote. The reports described preparations and internal discussions rather than an approved attack.
Previous fighting hit Bitcoin and U.S. markets
The conflict’s effect on oil and American financial markets was documented in a Sep. 1 market report. Following fresh U.S. strikes on Iranian targets, Bitcoin fell through $78,000 and $77,000 to trade around $76,762, down from an intraday high near $79,166.
According to CoinGlass figures cited in that report, roughly $115 million in leveraged crypto long positions were liquidated within one hour. Ethereum also fell below $2,400 during the selling.
Reuters figures included in the coverage showed Brent crude settling 4.6% higher at $94.65 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 5.2% to $90.22. The report also recorded rising Treasury yields and an S&P 500 decline to its lowest level since Aug. 4.
American investors’ exposure also runs through U.S.-listed Bitcoin funds. In its Sep. 28 coverage, the publication cited Farside Investors data showing $2.39 billion in net inflows into spot Bitcoin ETFs during Sep. 21–25. Every session recorded positive flows, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for about $1.16 billion.
An Aug. 31 market report documented another period when Bitcoin held near $77,900 despite renewed fighting and rising crude prices. According to that coverage, BTC gained approximately 23% during August, compared with reported monthly advances of 9% for gold and 4% for the Nasdaq.
The same report said U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs had accumulated about $2.8 billion across eight consecutive inflow sessions. Farside data cited in the coverage then showed an estimated $201.9 million in net outflows on Aug. 28.
Iran prepares its response to Washington’s proposal
Following Trump’s statement, Polymarket traders assigned a 60% probability that the U.S.-Iran ceasefire would remain in place through Nov. 15, according to the supplied report. PrimeXBT’s Oct. 8 coverage also recorded a 60% reading for the ceasefire lasting until mid-November.
On the diplomatic track, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran had submitted its seven-day plan and received Washington’s views in response, according to remarks reported by Antiwar.com, citing WANA.
The foreign minister said Iran was reviewing the American response and expected to answer within the next few days. In the same remarks, he warned that Tehran was more prepared than before if Washington pursued military action and would take measures to defend itself.

"We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran," Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social. "We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd."
The war, which began in February when the US and Israel launched strikes on Iran, has helped drive Trump's domestic approval ratings downward and is weighing heavily on his fellow Republicans as they seek to preserve their narrow legislative majorities in November's election.
Some 60% of Americans - including one in four Republicans - disapprove of how Trump is handling the situation in Iran, according to a recent Reuters/Ipsos poll. The conflict has pushed gasoline prices sharply higher at a time when voters say their top concern is the cost of living.

Proposals exchanged aimed at ending war, opening Strait of Hormuz
Iran and the US have exchanged proposals in recent weeks aimed at ending the war and reopening the Strait of Hormuz, a vital global energy shipping route. Trump rejected Tehran's latest offer.
Iran's state media reported on Thursday that Tehran would not abandon uranium enrichment or hand over its uranium stockpile, citing the head of the country's Atomic Energy Organization, days after US Vice President JD Vance told Reuters that Iran must make "meaningful" reductions in its enrichment capacity.
The US, Israel and Western allies have long accused Iran of seeking nuclear weapons, an accusation Iran has denied.
US imposes fresh sanctions on Iran's shadow fleet
The US imposed fresh sanctions on Iran on Thursday, targeting individuals, networks and 17 vessels for transporting Iranian crude, oil products and petrochemicals, the Treasury Department said, as Washington stepped up economic pressure on Tehran.
The sanctions are part of the department's "Operation Economic Outcast," which aims to cut Iran's funding for the war with the US, missile construction, cyberattacks and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, or IRGC.
"Today's action represents the most significant blow yet to Iran's remaining illicit maritime infrastructure by neutralizing the vast majority of the shadow fleet," a Treasury official told reporters on a call. "Treasury is cutting off the regime's last major source of illicit revenue and strengthening international pressure to hold Tehran accountable."
The move tightens the squeeze on Iranian oil sales after the US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14 following the breakdown of a memorandum of understanding between Tehran and Washington to end the war.
Iran has only about 20 million barrels of crude oil left on vessels outside the blockade, off Singapore, Malaysia and China, the Treasury official said. The world uses about 100 million barrels of oil per day.
A second Treasury official said Iran has stopped loading and offloading crude oil vessels due to the blockade and sanctions.
Trump said on social media on Thursday that the US is having "productive discussions" with Iran over the war that began on February 28. Trump said the US will not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
An analyst said the fact that the US is sanctioning vessels after Iran has delivered virtually all of its oil at sea means the impact will be muted.
"This is economic warfare conducted in the rearview mirror, designed to generate headlines rather than results," said Brett Erickson, a managing principal at Obsidian Risk Advisors.
Vessels targeted by the US sanctions include the Comoros-flagged Paritosh, the Panama-flagged Bitu, and the Bahamas-flagged Gas Lucky.

sources.text:
The Strait of Hormuz is not the whole map; it is only one part of the broader 2026 U.S.-Israel-Iran conflict, although it is a critical maritime chokepoint through which roughly 20 percent of the world’s oil and LNG transited before the conflict began.
U.S. airstrikes have spanned far beyond the strait, including strikes by the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) on military targets across Iranian territory such as Bushehr, Chah Bahar, Jask, Konarak, Abu Musa, and Bandar Abbas.
Iranian counter-attacks targeting U.S. and allied bases and assets in Bahrain, Jordan, and Kuwait, alongside major damage to regional energy and port infrastructure, as well as targeting ships traveling the Strait.
However, in a span of about 24 hours this week, two tankers were hit or set ablaze in waters that were supposed to be the safer side of this fight.
Euronews reported that the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said the Acers, an Antigua and Barbuda-flagged oil and chemical tanker, was hit by several projectiles on Wednesday about 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal, off Qatar’s northern coast.
There were casualties, though no numbers have been released.
It was the first attack in that stretch of the Gulf in more than six months.
A day later, a fire broke out aboard a tanker, likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout, roughly 40 kilometers off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman.
NASA’s FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze.
Two US KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft, and several helicopters were over the area at the time of the strike.
Neither ship was in the strait.
IRGC Begins Escalation Ahead Of November 3
IRGC-affiliated outlets have hinted that operations against vessels Iran considers in “violation” of its rules now extend beyond Hormuz.
IRGC-affiliated media outlets said Tehran has “extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait.”
“Our missiles determine the distance between you and us,” Acting Defense Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
“Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs.
If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines,” ol-Reza added.
This is the opening gambit to influence the US midterm elections.
This Is About The Workaround
So why would Iran attack outside the strait now? Follow the oil.
Despite Iran’s best efforts to stop oil from flowing via the Strait, due to US airstrikes, its hold is beginning to loosen.
According to Al Jazeera, Gulf oil flows outside of Iran recovered to more than 81 percent of pre-war levels in September, citing Kpler data, and roughly 40 percent of petroleum exports now bypass the strait altogether.
Saudi Arabia is transporting oil through its East-West pipeline to Yanbu on the Red Sea, while shuttle tankers run ship-to-ship transfers near the strait with their transponders switched off.
The location where the Dhalgout was burning is important.
Fujairah is the UAE’s major export outlet on the Gulf of Oman, the endpoint of a pipeline Abu Dhabi built so it wouldn’t have to hold its oil hostage at Hormuz.
A tanker on fire 40 kilometers from the port sends a message to every shipping company and insurance underwriter that the bypass isn’t safe either.
Iran is desperately trying to disrupt the flow of oil, thereby boosting prices before November. Shipping intelligence firm Marisks counted at least seven tanker incidents in a single week.
The UKMTO has logged at least one attack a day in the Strait of Hormuz or the Gulf of Aden since October 2, where the Iranian proxy Houthis are targeting Saudi-linked shipping.
All of which has helped raise oil prices.
The Threats Are Getting Bigger Too
Tehran’s rhetoric is stretching to match the geography.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to the missing Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, warned this week that Iran could take the war into the Indian Ocean if the U.S. or Israel strikes again, which is a not-so-veiled threat against Diego Garcia.
Iranian bluster has always been a cornerstone of their media.
However, that’s beside the point.
The IRGC has spent seven months proving it can hit commercial shipping, and it hasn’t needed a navy to do it.
A Huge Mistake: Trump Just Handed Tehran A Window
The timing took an ugly turn.
On the same day the Dhalgout was attacked, President Trump posted on Truth Social that the U.S. would not attack Iran before the midterm elections on November 3.
That was a huge mistake.
One of the first things you learn in a conflict is that you never tell the other side when you won’t hit them.
Uncertainty is a weapon.
Tehran now feels it has a 26-day window of opportunity, with its own soil off-limits until after the midterms, and tankers off Qatar and Fujairah as the low-hanging fruit.
The Navy can still escort, intercept, and shoot down incoming drones.
However, presence alone isn’t deterrence.
When the Dhalgout was hit, U.S. aircraft were already overhead. None of that stopped it.
The Honest Trade-Off
So is Iran expanding the conflict?
Yes.
However, it’s a calibrated expansion.
Tehran is hitting merchant ships, not American warships.
It isn’t claiming the attacks outright. It’s keeping the casualty counts low enough to avoid handing Washington an excuse to break its own pledge.
The goal is simple.
Make the workaround as expensive and as dangerous as the strait itself, and squeeze the global economy until someone in Washington blinks, and then claim aggrieved status with the US as the aggressor.
Every tanker that is attacked in the Gulf adds to that bill, and to the price at the pump three weeks before Americans vote.
The Strait of Hormuz was never the whole map. Tehran is now testing the waters to see if it can influence the US population to vote for it.

sources.news_title: Trump Rules Out Iran Strikes Before November Midterms, Says Nuclear Negotiations Are Making Progress
sources.text:
President Donald Trump has pledged to halt additional military attacks against Iran until after the Nov. 3 elections, contradicting reports that the Pentagon was preparing new strikes while reaffirming that Tehran must abandon any pursuit of nuclear weapons.
By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump announced Thursday, Oct. 8, that the United States will not conduct additional military strikes against Iran before the November midterm elections, declaring that diplomatic negotiations are progressing despite Washington’s continued economic blockade and disagreements over Tehran’s nuclear enrichment activities.
The announcement followed reports that the White House had requested military options for renewed attacks against Iranian targets before Americans vote Nov. 3. Trump rejected the prospect of immediate military escalation while maintaining that Iran must not be permitted to develop a nuclear weapon.
The president’s statement represents a significant public commitment to restrain military operations during the remaining weeks of the election campaign, although it does not rule out additional strikes after Election Day.
In a statement published Thursday morning on Truth Social, Trump described continuing discussions with Iranian officials and cited increased oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz as evidence that American economic and military pressure was producing results.
“We are having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran. I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition, both Economically and Militarily, and while the Blockade will remain in full force and effect, with Oil flowing in Record Numbers of Barrels through the Hormuz Strait (22 Million Barrels, last night alone, with not one barrel coming from, or going to, Iran!), we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd. IRAN WILL NOT HAVE A NUCLEAR WEAPON! President DONALD J. TRUMP”
The president’s full statement was also circulated as the administration sought to clarify its position following speculation about renewed military action.
Trump’s declaration came less than a day after The Atlantic reported that the White House had requested military strike options targeting Iran before the midterm elections.
The magazine cited two administration officials familiar with the planning, who said the Pentagon had been directed to prepare possible operations while senior officials debated whether additional strikes would advance American objectives.
According to the report, the administration was considering military action that could demonstrate progress in the conflict and potentially influence energy prices before the election.
The proposed operations were not described as having received final presidential authorization.
The Atlantic reported that the size, objectives and timing of any additional attacks remained under discussion, with some officials favoring military action and others concerned about the consequences of escalating the conflict during the final weeks of the campaign.
The report stated that the administration had been considering a resumption of hostilities after several weeks without direct American strikes against Iranian targets.
“After months of on-again, off-again fighting, the United States hasn’t struck Iran in several weeks,” the magazine reported. “The stretch of relative tranquility is coinciding with the final phase of the midterm-election campaign, and the assumption has been that President Trump will want to keep it going through November 3 so as not to remind voters of an unpopular war that is dragging Republican candidates down nationwide.”
The article then described the possibility that the administration was considering a different course.
“But that may not be what happens. The White House has asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be exercised ahead of the midterms, according to two administration officials. The planning underscores just how much the president wants to reduce gas prices and demonstrate progress in the conflict before the vote, administration officials told us.”
The military planning was also confirmed in separate reporting by Axios, which said the Pentagon had instructed U.S. Central Command to complete preparations for potentially resuming major combat operations.
Officials described possible strikes against Iranian energy infrastructure, military installations and nuclear facilities, although no final decision had been made.
A Pentagon official emphasized that developing military options is part of the department’s normal responsibility to provide the president with operational choices.
The administration’s position Thursday therefore distinguishes between maintaining military readiness and authorizing a new attack.
Trump has previously emphasized his willingness to use military force if negotiations fail, but his latest statement establishes that he does not intend to order additional strikes before Nov. 3.
The announcement comes during an extended conflict that has disrupted international energy markets, increased military tensions across the Middle East and generated concerns about the security of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The narrow waterway between Iran and Oman is one of the world’s most important maritime energy routes, connecting oil-producing countries around the Persian Gulf with international markets.
Disruptions to shipping through the strait can affect global petroleum supplies, transportation costs and gasoline prices in the United States.
The administration has pursued a blockade intended to restrict Iranian oil exports while permitting other commercial vessels to continue using the route.
Trump said Thursday that 22 million barrels of oil had passed through the strait the previous night, with none originating from or destined for Iran.
The figure was presented by the president as evidence that Washington was maintaining pressure on Tehran while allowing substantial quantities of petroleum to reach international markets.
Independent verification of the precise overnight shipment total was not immediately available.
The administration’s strategy combines restrictions on Iranian oil commerce with efforts to protect shipping and negotiate an agreement addressing Tehran’s nuclear activities.
Iran has resisted American demands involving uranium enrichment and has repeatedly argued that it possesses the right to pursue civilian nuclear energy.
Washington maintains that Iran’s enrichment activities must be restricted sufficiently to prevent the production of nuclear weapons.
That disagreement remains the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement.
Vice President JD Vance reinforced the administration’s position during an exclusive interview with Reuters published Tuesday, Oct. 6.
Vance said Tehran would have to make a meaningful reduction in its nuclear enrichment capabilities before the United States could accept a final agreement ending the conflict.
The vice president specifically questioned why Iran would continue producing uranium enriched to approximately 60% purity if its nuclear program were intended exclusively for peaceful purposes.
Uranium enriched to that level is substantially above the concentration generally required for civilian nuclear power generation, although additional processing would be necessary to reach weapons-grade enrichment.
“If you don’t want a nuclear weapon, then why do you need 60% enriched fuel? And if you want to show commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, don’t build highly enriched fuel. That’s a very basic threshold issue,” Vance said.
“I think if they want to show a commitment to not building a nuclear weapon, they would do something meaningful on their enrichment capacity.”
Vance’s remarks established that the administration considers reductions in uranium enrichment a central requirement for ending the war.
Iranian officials have maintained that their nuclear activities are intended for peaceful purposes and that the country’s right to enrich uranium should be recognized.
The disagreement has persisted despite months of negotiations involving American, Iranian and regional representatives.
Vance acknowledged that the administration faces difficulties identifying which Iranian officials possess final authority to make binding decisions.
Changes in Iran’s leadership following earlier military operations have complicated negotiations, according to U.S. officials, who have expressed uncertainty about the internal decision-making process in Tehran.
The vice president said that uncertainty makes it more difficult to determine whether proposed agreements will be accepted and implemented.
Diplomatic efforts have also been affected by disputes over the extent of sanctions relief, the status of Iran’s nuclear materials and the future of American restrictions on Iranian oil exports.
The current negotiations follow an earlier round of talks that appeared to offer an opportunity for reducing hostilities before breaking down.
The United States and Iran previously reached a provisional agreement in June, but the arrangement failed to produce a lasting settlement.
Additional discussions mediated by Qatar subsequently sought to restore diplomatic progress.
In late September, representatives from Washington and Tehran participated in another round of negotiations that initially appeared constructive.
However, differences between the parties became apparent as the discussions concluded.
Trump subsequently indicated that the United States would not make further concessions on its principal demands.
In a statement issued following the negotiations, the president said Washington had maintained its position and would not abandon its requirements for a satisfactory agreement.
The diplomatic setback was followed by reports that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had directed Iranian representatives to leave the United States after the talks ended.
According to Axios’ account of the negotiations and the Iranian delegation’s departure, the decision reflected frustration within the administration over the failure to achieve meaningful progress.
The report described a breakdown in discussions after American and Iranian representatives were unable to bridge differences concerning the terms of a potential agreement.
The nuclear enrichment dispute was among the central issues, although officials did not publicly establish that it was the sole reason the negotiations stalled.
The exchanges occurred against the backdrop of increasingly forceful warnings from Trump.
On Sept. 30, the president threatened additional military action if Tehran refused to accept Washington’s terms.
In remarks reported by Politico, Trump suggested that the United States could launch devastating attacks against Iran if diplomatic efforts failed.
The threat illustrated the administration’s willingness to use the possibility of renewed military operations as leverage in negotiations.
Trump’s Thursday announcement does not withdraw the broader threat of future action, but it establishes a specific period during which the president says additional attacks will not occur.
The administration has maintained that Iran’s nuclear program remains a national security concern despite the American military operation conducted in June 2025.
During that operation, known as Operation Midnight Hammer, U.S. forces struck three major Iranian nuclear facilities: Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan.
The military campaign involved long-range American bombers and precision weapons intended to damage deeply protected infrastructure associated with Iran’s nuclear activities.
The operation included B-2 Spirit stealth bombers equipped with specialized bunker-penetrating munitions designed to destroy hardened underground facilities.
American forces also used submarine-launched cruise missiles as part of the coordinated attacks.
The Pentagon described the mission as a major success, and Trump repeatedly asserted that the strikes had destroyed Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
The president publicly characterized the operation as having devastated Iran’s nuclear program, arguing that the facilities targeted were central to Tehran’s ability to produce nuclear weapons.
Independent assessments of the long-term damage have been more cautious, however, distinguishing the destruction of physical infrastructure from the elimination of nuclear materials, technical knowledge and the ability to rebuild enrichment facilities.
The administration’s continued insistence on restrictions involving Iran’s uranium enrichment demonstrates that the nuclear issue remains unresolved.
Iran has not agreed to abandon the enrichment capabilities demanded by Washington, while American officials continue to consider the possibility of additional military operations if negotiations fail.
The conflict has also placed considerable pressure on international oil markets.
The Strait of Hormuz has experienced repeated disruptions involving commercial shipping, and restrictions on Iranian petroleum exports have added to uncertainty over global supply.
Energy markets have reacted to reports of possible renewed military action, with oil prices climbing sharply Thursday amid concerns about Middle East tensions and temporary production shutdowns associated with Hurricane Isaias in the Gulf of Mexico.
Brent crude rose above $105 per barrel, reflecting increased concern among traders about potential supply disruptions.
Rising petroleum prices have become a political concern for the administration as American voters evaluate the cost of gasoline and other household expenses ahead of the midterm elections.
The Atlantic reported that some administration officials believed renewed military action could demonstrate progress in the conflict and potentially improve the outlook for energy prices.
Others reportedly questioned whether additional strikes would produce those results, warning that military escalation could instead increase instability and push oil prices higher.
That disagreement reflects the complicated relationship between military operations, shipping security and global energy supply.
Attacks on Iranian infrastructure could reduce Tehran’s ability to conduct military operations, but they could also provoke retaliation against commercial vessels, regional facilities or American military installations.
The possibility of additional strikes has also raised security concerns among American allies.
Recent intelligence warnings involving U.S. bases in Europe have highlighted fears that Iranian operatives or affiliated groups could target American military infrastructure outside the Middle East.
American and European authorities have reportedly increased monitoring of potential threats against facilities supporting U.S. operations.

Trump says he will not attack Iran before the midterm election
By Alayna Treene, Kevin Liptak, CNN
(CNN) — President Donald Trump announced Thursday that he has no plans to strike Iran before the midterm election.
“We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” Trump declared on Truth Social, adding that the administration is “having productive discussions” with Tehran and that his main goal is to ensure the country does not obtain a nuclear weapon.
The president’s comments come after multiple media reports detailed the administration planning for potential new strikes before the elections — just 26 days away.
Trump emphasized that he plans to keep up economic pressure on Iran, saying the blockade of Iranian ports “will remain in full force and effect.” The administration has favored economic punishment over military strikes for months, though it’s seemingly done little to motivate Iranian officials to negotiate.
The Treasury Department announced additional sanctions against Iran on Thursday, impacting 17 vessels that officials alleged were part of a “shadow fleet” that Iran has used to ship its oil around the world. The department concluded that they had circumvented existing US sanctions to transport millions of barrels of oil and other petrochemical products to countries across south and east Asia.
“Treasury is targeting any source of the regime’s illicit revenue, as well as its sanctions evasion schemes to move funds,” the department said in its statement announcing the new sanctions.
Trump has suggested in campaign trail remarks over the last several weeks that he is considering new military action on Iran, telling supporters he has a decision in front of him on how to proceed.
While other administration officials have claimed the war is essentially over, Trump said this week the US still has unfinished business.
“They’re a mess. But we still have to finish it off,” he said during remarks at a new shipyard in Maryland on Tuesday.
The US president has appeared reluctant to resume the war in earnest before the midterms, however, mindful of the political downsides that could come with renewing an already unpopular conflict. Officials also know that flareups between the US and Iran have caused spikes in oil prices, aggravating cost-of-living concerns that have dragged down Trump’s Republican allies.
Still, the president had not entirely ruled out resuming military strikes before the midterms until his post on social media Thursday, according to officials familiar with the matter. They said American military planners have been preparing options for a resumption of hostilities, including targeting Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear targets.
Trump and top national security officials have held extensive discussions about the next steps in Iran as they work to find a way to get more ships moving through the Strait of Hormuz. Top administration officials traveled to Camp David last Friday for a discussion on Iran, including longer-term planning on the war, officials said.
Trump’s claim of “productive discussions” with Iran came after the president rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last month.
Since then, the US has sent a counterproposal that Tehran says it is considering. An Iranian news agency reported Thursday that Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said officials planned to respond “within the next few days.”

President Donald Trump said Thursday that the U.S. will not attack Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm election, explicitly tying the timing of potential further military action to the domestic political calendar.
"We will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections," Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the U.S. was having "productive discussions" with Tehran.
Trump's declaration came after he told reporters late Wednesday that his administration was considering renewed strikes against Tehran before the election, helping send oil prices higher amid fears of further escalation. Brent crude rose more than 4% Thursday to above $104 a barrel.
Trump said the U.S. naval blockade of Iran would remain in place and reiterated that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.
It's a shift from his posture less than a day ago. At a campaign rally Wednesday night, Trump said a deal with Iran was "not really something that I wanted to do."
The more diplomatic tone comes as voters are already casting midterm ballots and public support for the war has fallen. Just 31% of Americans supported U.S. military action against Iran in an August Reuters/Ipsos poll, down from 37% in March, while 83% expected the conflict to be prolonged.
The war has helped push fuel costs higher, compounding Republicans' vulnerability on affordability as they fight to retain control of Congress. Poll after poll has ranked the cost of living among voters' top concerns heading into the Nov. 3 election.
Gas prices have climbed roughly 40% from a year ago, according to AAA data. The national average stood at $4.36 a gallon Thursday, up from $2.98 just before war began in late February.
The political fallout is showing up on the campaign trail. Numerous GOP candidates in competitive congressional races have tried to distance themselves from Trump, often on the Iran war.

Reuters reported in September that top Trump aides were pushing to keep the war contained through the midterms to limit Republican losses, while leaving open heavier U.S. strikes after votes are tallied.

sources.text:
President Donald Trump said Thursday the United States will not resume military strikes on Iran before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, even as the Pentagon keeps pushing more warships and troops toward the region and American drivers keep absorbing the cost of a war that has dragged on for months. Trump described his administration's ongoing talks with Tehran as productive, while Iranian officials said they had received a new U.S. counterproposal and expected to respond within days.
Trump Says Talks Are Productive, Leaves Door Open After Election
Trump said the United States will not order a resumption of military strikes on Iran before the midterm elections, which are set for Nov. 3, according to chicagotribune.com. He said his team has been having productive discussions with the Islamic Republic of Iran, and he hinted he was confident an endgame to the war could arrive in the days just before or after the election. Even so, the outlet reported that Trump remained open to resuming full-scale military operations against Iran once the vote has passed.
On the diplomatic track, Iranian officials said Tehran had received a U.S. counterproposal, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran expected to offer a formal reply within days, per the same report. That exchange follows a rockier patch in September, when the Trump administration rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the U.S. met certain conditions — a stretch during which negotiations between the two countries appeared to be at a standstill.
A Third Carrier Strike Group Heads to the Region
Even as Trump talks up diplomacy, the military buildup hasn't slowed. The U.S. is dispatching a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, including the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious readiness group, according to The Guardian. Those ships together carry more than 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines, the paper reported, and a U.S. official said three carriers could be in the region as early as the end of October.
The Theodore Roosevelt and the thousands of troops aboard it and accompanying ships could arrive in the region by that same timeframe, the Chicago Tribune reported, citing the broader buildup of forces the U.S. military has dispatched to the Middle East. Trump also said the U.S. naval blockade of Iran would remain in place and that Tehran would not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, according to CNBC. Separately, The Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to develop strike options against Iranian targets that could be used before the midterms, with plans being developed by U.S. Central Command — though the size, targets and whether the administration will ultimately proceed remain under debate, according to The Atlantic.
USS Lincoln Comes Home After a Record 265 Days at Sea
One symbol of the war's toll pulled into San Diego Thursday. The USS Abraham Lincoln returned home after supporting the Iran war during a record-long deployment of 265 uninterrupted days at sea, according to NPR. Per a Presidential Unit Citation cited by the outlet, the Lincoln and its strike group executed 3,693 combat missions, delivered 1.37 million pounds of ordnance and launched 450 Tomahawk cruise missiles during the deployment.
The cost to the crew was steep. NPR reported that the Navy told lawmakers eight sailors attempted suicide during the record-setting deployment, and that the Lincoln's crew experienced stress and poor mental health, along with supply shortages that included food and hygiene products. The Lincoln had been relieved in Asia by the USS George Washington in August, while the USS George H.W. Bush — deployed in the Middle East for about six months — pulled into Phuket, Thailand, for a port visit this month, according to the Associated Press report carried by WOWT.
Gas Prices Climb as Public Support for Strikes Falls
The war's economic bite shows up most visibly at the pump. The national average gasoline price stood at $4.36 a gallon Thursday, up from $2.98 before the war began in late February, CNBC reported. AAA's average was $4.37 a gallon on October 7 and $4.36 on October 8.
Oil markets reacted directly to Trump's remarks. Brent crude had risen to about $105 a barrel before Trump's post announcing no strikes before the midterms, then dropped to $103 a barrel afterward, according to CBS News. CNBC reported that Brent crude had risen more than 4% Thursday to above $104 a barrel, and noted that crude prices have typically climbed whenever the U.S. has resumed strikes after a pause, per the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Public appetite for continued fighting has cooled alongside those costs. An August Reuters/Ipsos poll found just 31% of Americans supported U.S. military action against Iran, down from 37% in March, according to CNBC's report. The same poll found that 83% of Americans expected the conflict to be prolonged, underscoring the political weight hanging over Trump's promise to hold off on new strikes until after voters go to the polls Nov. 3.
